text: You get the root of a binary search tree, and a value, val. Insert that value into the tree and return the new root. The tree must still be a valid BST after you are done.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the tree is already a valid BST. So for every node, everything on the left is smaller, and everything on the right is bigger. I need to add one new value and keep that true. Is that right?
That's right.

Then here is the thing I want to say early, because it shapes the whole solution. The BST rule already tells me where the value goes. Each compare sends me left or right, so there is only one place I can stop — and it is always an empty slot. So the new node is always a leaf, and I never move an old node.
Two more questions. Can the tree be empty? And is val guaranteed to not be in the tree already?
Yes, the root can be null. And yes, val is guaranteed not to be there. All values are unique.
Good, that helps. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth nodes. Values and val are between minus ten to the eighth and ten to the eighth.

Noted. Ten thousand nodes is small, but the tree can be one long chain, so the depth can be ten thousand too. I'll come back to that when I talk about the stack. Let me run through the example: forty, twenty, sixty, ten, thirty, fifty, seventy, with val twenty-five. Twenty-five goes left of forty, right of twenty, then left of thirty — and that slot is empty. So twenty-five becomes the left child of thirty. That matches the expected answer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to read every value into a sorted list, add val, and rebuild a balanced BST. That is correct, but linear time and linear extra space, and it reshapes a tree that was already fine. This problem reminds me of a plain binary search, just on a tree instead of an array. Each compare drops one whole side — except when I run out of tree, I build a node instead of returning not found. So I'll do a simple recursive descent.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is null, return a new node holding val. Two: otherwise compare, and recurse into the left or right child. Three: store what that call returns back into the child, then return the node. One thing worth flagging — that store is not decoration, it is the wiring. The recursive call only got a copy of the parent's child pointer, so the new node has no other way into the tree. Drop the store and the node leaks while the tree stays unchanged. There's a trade-off here. A loop with a parent pointer uses constant space; the recursion costs order h stack. I'll take the recursion because it is easier to read, and check the stack math at the end. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it up.

Alright, let me code this up. A null root is the empty slot, so I return a new node. Otherwise the comparison picks a side, and I store the recursive result back into that child before returning root. One thing worth flagging — on the way back up, only one of those stores saves something new. In our example, thirty's left becoming twenty-five is the real one; twenty's right and forty's left just put back pointers that were already there. But I cannot know in advance which level is the real one, so every level needs the store.
I've seen people write that same pattern in the invert-tree problem. Is it always needed?

No, and that is a good contrast. In invert binary tree the write-back looks the same, but it is redundant. That recursion only swaps fields on existing nodes and always returns the pointer it was handed, so storing it back is a no-op. Over all six hundred twenty-six tree shapes with up to seven nodes, dropping it there changes zero results. Here, dropping it breaks four thousand seven hundred six out of four thousand seven hundred seven cases — only the empty tree survives. So my test is one question: can this recursion create a new node, or swap in a different subtree root? If yes, the write-back is the wiring. If no, it is decoration.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Forty, twenty, sixty, ten, thirty, fifty, seventy, with val twenty-five — I expect it as the left child of thirty. The row that matters is the fourth call: it lands on null and allocates the node, and storing it into thirty's left is the only write that changes anything. Four calls, one allocation — calls equal the depth of the new leaf plus one. That matches. Corner cases: an empty tree returns the new node in one call. A value smaller than everything hangs off the leftmost node; bigger, off the rightmost. A right-leaning chain walks the whole chain.

The time complexity is order h, where h is the height — one compare per level, and I never look at a sibling. The space complexity is order h for the call stack, plus the one node I allocate. In the worst-case scenario the tree is one long chain, so h equals n and both become linear. If the tree is balanced, it's log n. Let me think about complexity here — specifically the stack, since that worst case is real at ten thousand nodes.

One thing I want to be precise about: this is not a tail call. After the recursive call comes back, I still store the result and return root, so the compiler cannot turn it into a jump. In the arm64 assembly at O2, it's a real call followed by the store. So O2 only shrinks the frame, to thirty-two bytes per level. On an eight megabyte stack, the crash depth is about two hundred sixty-one thousand at O2, and about a hundred four thousand at O0. Ten thousand levels fits easily. But with a five hundred twelve kilobyte stack, the O0 build segfaults at ten thousand while O2 survives. So on a thread with a small stack, I'd switch to the iterative version.

Oh, one more thing — I want to make one assumption explicit. I wrote greater-than and less-than, which leaves the equal case doing nothing. That is only safe because val is promised not to be in the tree, so greater-or-equal would behave identically here. If duplicates were allowed, I would need a rule — send them right, or keep a count on the node — and I'd ask about that before coding.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why the write-back is load-bearing — the new node has no path back into the parent — and gave the invert-tree contrast plus a clean test for telling the cases apart. You noticed only one store on the path is real, but you can't know which one ahead of time. And you checked the tail-call question in the actual assembly, and turned it into a real stack budget. Good work.
